title: Unusual iron in Chang’e-6 soil could record ancient lunar magnetism
summary:
A tiny particle inside lunar glass could carry a record of a much larger world. Researchers studying Chang’e-6 soil have identified an unusual form of iron that may help scientists investigate the Moon’s ancient magnetic environment.

The Moon no longer generates a global magnetic field. However, magnetic minerals in its rocks and soil can preserve traces of earlier conditions. Reading those traces helps researchers reconstruct how the Moon’s magnetism changed over time.

The study, led by Haifeng Du at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, examined metallic iron embedded in two impact-glass samples. Impact glass forms when a collision melts material that later cools into glass. The team used focused ion beam preparation, electron microscopy and chemical analysis to inspect particles on a nanoscale, far below what our eyes can see.

They identified face-centered cubic gamma iron, written as γ-Fe, for the first time in natural lunar samples. The name describes the arrangement of atoms within the material. Gamma iron was the dominant iron form in the two samples studied. That finding does not mean it is the dominant form across all lunar soil.

The discovery presents a puzzle. Under normal conditions, gamma iron is stable only at high temperatures. During cooling, it usually transforms into alpha iron, another atomic arrangement. Yet gamma iron remained in the lunar glass.

The researchers proposed several possible explanations. Small amounts of carbon and other elements could help stabilize it. Molten material may also have cooled rapidly after an impact, while the surrounding glass could protect the particles. These are proposed contributing factors, rather than a fully settled explanation.

Relatively large gamma-iron particles could form a stable magnetic pattern called a single vortex. They also maintained a consistent magnetic response when exposed to an outside magnetic field. That stability suggests they might preserve information about earlier magnetic conditions.

Gamma iron and alpha iron form under different conditions and behave differently magnetically. They could therefore record separate stages of a lunar impact event, giving researchers more than one kind of evidence to compare.

Published on September 16 in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, the study expands the known range of magnetic materials in lunar samples. Further work must establish exactly what these particles can reveal about the Moon’s ancient field and its evolution.
why_it_matters: The discovery expands the magnetic materials scientists can study in lunar samples. Gamma iron could preserve clues from stages of impact events that differ from those recorded by alpha iron.
